title: Session / cookies
summary: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, fixation, logout, and session identifiers in URLs.

groups.title: Cookie flags
groups.summary: How the session cookie is issued.

checks.title: Secure on session cookies
checks.why: A session cookie without Secure can be stolen on a plaintext request.
checks.validate: Set-Cookie for the session name lacks Secure on the real login response.

variants.name: Read Set-Cookie on login
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password=ChangeMe1!
variants.expect: Every cookie that carries authority must include Secure. Repeat on the first 302.
variants.why: The Secure flag on the session cookie is the transport protection.

variants.name: HTTP Set-Cookie
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: A session cookie issued on HTTP is worse. Confirm on port 80 only if HTTP is in scope.
variants.why: A session cookie issued over plaintext HTTP can be stolen on the network.

checks.title: HttpOnly on session cookies
checks.why: A session cookie readable by JavaScript becomes XSS→session theft.
checks.validate: document.cookie contains the session name, or Set-Cookie lacks HttpOnly.

variants.name: Read Set-Cookie
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password=ChangeMe1!
variants.expect: Session cookies must include HttpOnly. CSRF tokens may be readable; session ids must not.
variants.why: HttpOnly keeps the session cookie out of script reach.

variants.name: document.cookie
variants.payload: In the logged-in origin console: document.cookie
variants.expect: The session name must be absent. Any other privileged cookie you can read is the same class.
variants.why: A session cookie readable from document.cookie is exposed to any XSS.

checks.title: SameSite matches the real flow
checks.why: SameSite=None without Secure, or Lax when a cross-site POST is the login/CSRF surface.
checks.validate: The issued cookie's SameSite does not match how the app actually authenticates.

variants.name: Read SameSite
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password=ChangeMe1!
variants.expect: None requires Secure. Strict breaks top-level OAuth returns. Lax is the usual default — still need a CSRF token on POST.
variants.why: SameSite binds the cookie to the request's site context.

variants.name: Cross-site POST with Lax
variants.payload:
<form action="https://www.example.com/account/email" method="POST">
  <input name="email" value="attacker@example.com">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
variants.expect: Lax should not send the cookie on this POST in modern browsers. A change still happening means the cookie is None or not SameSite.
variants.why: Lax still allows top-level cross-site POSTs, so it is not a CSRF control by itself.

groups.title: Lifecycle
groups.summary: Fixation, logout, and identifiers in URLs.

checks.title: Session fixation / rotation
checks.why: A pre-login cookie that survives authentication lets an attacker plant the session.
checks.validate: The session identifier issued before login is still accepted after login.

variants.name: Compare pre- and post-login cookies
variants.payload: Note Set-Cookie on GET /login, submit credentials, compare the cookie name and value.
variants.expect: Value must change. A new name with the old value still counting is the same bug.
variants.why: The session id must rotate on login; a stable id is the fixation primitive.

variants.name: Planted cookie
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Cookie: session=wapt-planted-value
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password=ChangeMe1!
variants.expect: The planted value must not become the authenticated session.
variants.why: Accepting a pre-set session cookie after login means the server did not issue a fresh one.

checks.title: Logout invalidates the server session
checks.why: Logout only deletes the cookie. The old value still works.
checks.validate: A replayed session cookie after logout still returns /me.

variants.name: Replay after logout
variants.payload: Copy the session cookie, log out, send GET /api/v1/me with the old cookie.
variants.expect: Must 401. A 200 is the finding.
variants.why: A session that still works after logout means server-side invalidation is missing.

variants.name: Logout CSRF / missing logout
variants.payload:
<form action="https://www.example.com/logout" method="POST"></form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
variants.expect: Forced logout is a finding if there is no CSRF token. Missing logout entirely is a finding too.
variants.why: A missing or CSRF-able logout lets an attacker silently end or hijack the session.

checks.title: Session id in the URL
checks.why: jsessionid=, PHPSESSID=, or a token in the path/query lands in logs and Referer.
checks.validate: A live session identifier is observable in a URL or Referer.

variants.name: Path / query session
variants.payload:
GET /app;jsessionid=<value> HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Rewriting session ids into the URL must be off. Also try ?PHPSESSID= and ?session=.
variants.why: A session id in the URL leaks into logs, history, and Referer.

variants.name: Referer leak
variants.payload: If any URL contains the session id, load a third-party image and inspect Referer.
variants.expect: The identifier must not leave the origin.
variants.why: A session id in the URL reaches a third party via the Referer header.

checks.title: Every session token inventoried
checks.why: You cannot reason about session security for tokens you have not enumerated — most fixation and leakage findings start with a forgotten second cookie.
checks.validate: A written inventory of every identity-bearing value: name, transport (cookie/header/body/URL), set at which request, and cleared when.

variants.name: Full-login capture
variants.payload: Burp Proxy on; log in, navigate, refresh, step-up, and log out. Filter Set-Cookie and Authorization. Record every value that appears or changes with identity.
variants.expect: Table of tokens with transport and lifecycle. Values redacted in evidence.
variants.why: One clean capture beats guesswork about what carries identity.

variants.name: Removal test
variants.payload: For each candidate token, remove it (one at a time) on a harmless authenticated request and re-issue.
variants.expect: Only the documented primary token matters; removing auxiliaries (CSRF, device, preference) changes only their own behaviour.
variants.why: Proves which values independently restore authenticated state.

variants.name: URL and storage sweep
variants.payload: Search the proxy history for the token value appearing in URLs, Referer headers, or script-readable storage; check DevTools Application tab.
variants.expect: Session authority never appears in URLs, Referer-bearing navigation, localStorage, or non-HttpOnly cookies.
variants.why: Where a token lives decides what can read it.

checks.title: Cookie Domain and Path scoped tight
checks.why: A cookie scoped to the parent domain or site root is handed to every sibling application and path — session soup across trust boundaries.
checks.validate: Session cookies set Domain only when required (narrowest host) and the minimal Path; no host-only bypasses.

variants.name: Read the Set-Cookie scope
variants.payload: After login, read Domain and Path attributes of every session cookie.
variants.expect: Host-only cookies (no Domain) with Path at the app root or narrower; any Domain=.example.com on session authority is a finding.
variants.why: The attribute pair is the blast radius.

variants.name: Sibling acceptance
variants.payload: If Domain is parent-scoped, open a sibling subdomain in scope and check document.cookie (or the request) for the session cookie.
variants.expect: Sibling must never see or send session authority; report with the exact attribute evidence.
variants.why: Parent scoping shares sessions with every subdomain, including less-hardened ones.

variants.name: Path creep
variants.payload: Request a static asset path outside the application and observe whether the session cookie rides along.
variants.expect: Path-limited cookies stay within the app scope; site-wide paths need justification.
variants.why: Broad paths leak authority into lower-trust handlers.

checks.title: Persistent lifetime matches need
checks.why: "Remember me" that never forgets turns a stolen cookie into permanent access.
checks.validate: Persistent cookies only on explicit remember-me, with documented lifetimes; ordinary sessions are session-cookies.

variants.name: Attribute read
variants.payload: After a normal login, inspect Expires/Max-Age on session cookies without touching remember-me.
variants.expect: Ordinary auth sets session cookies (no Expires); only the remember-me cookie is persistent.
variants.why: Persistence should be a choice, not a default.

variants.name: Remember-me horizon
variants.payload: Enable remember-me and read its lifetime.
variants.expect: Days-to-weeks, consistent with policy; multi-month or multi-year lifetimes are findings.
variants.why: The horizon is the theft window.

variants.name: Persistence downgrade
variants.payload: Log out from a remember-me session and re-check storage and replay.
variants.expect: Remember-me material is invalidated server-side on logout, not just deleted client-side.
variants.why: A logged-out cookie that still works defeats the logout.

checks.title: Reference tokens carry real entropy
checks.why: Sequential, short, or structured session ids are brute-forceable or guessable across accounts.
checks.validate: Opaque ids are at least 128 bits of randomness: same length, mixed charset, no visible pattern across accounts.

variants.name: Multi-account sample
variants.payload: Log in as your two test accounts several times (and refresh); collect 10+ session ids.
variants.expect: Ids never repeat, share prefixes, or reveal sequence; lengths and charsets are stable and long (20+ chars mixed).
variants.why: Your own accounts give a safe, legal sample.

variants.name: Structure decode
variants.payload: Base64/hex-decode ids where they look encoded; look for embedded username, uid, or timestamp.
variants.expect: Ids are opaque; any embedded identity or counter structure is documented (pattern-guessable is a finding).
variants.why: Encoding is not entropy — decoding often shows structure.

variants.name: Pre-auth id
variants.payload: Compare anonymous (pre-login) session id vs post-login id.
variants.expect: Different values and different authority after login; an id that survives login is fixation surface.
variants.why: Pre-auth ids must never become post-auth authority.

checks.title: No sensitive plaintext in tokens
checks.why: Client-visible tokens that carry passwords, PII, or secrets leak them to every place the token travels (logs, Referer, storage, XSS).
checks.validate: Decoded token contents contain only opaque identifiers; no credentials, PII, or internal secrets.

variants.name: Decode and read
variants.payload: Decode each identity cookie (base64/base64url/hex/JWT) and read the claims.
variants.expect: Opaque ids only; document any readable fields. Roles/tenant in a client-mutable token must be server-verified.
variants.why: Reading your own session token is the fastest content audit.

variants.name: Sensitive-value grep
variants.payload: Grep decoded tokens (and the whole cookie jar) for the test password, username, email, and internal hostnames from your engagement notes.
variants.expect: Zero hits for credentials or PII.
variants.why: If you can find the password in the cookie, so can every log line.

variants.name: Known-secret canary
variants.payload: Set a canary value via profile fields you control (display name), then re-read tokens.
variants.expect: Canary absent from all tokens — user content must not be mirrored into authority material.
variants.why: Proves the token is not a dump of account state.

checks.title: Session rotates on authentication
checks.why: A session id that survives login lets an attacker plant a pre-auth id (fixation) and ride it into the victim account.
checks.validate: A fresh session id is issued at every privilege transition: anonymous to authenticated, and at each re-authentication.

variants.name: Before/after compare
variants.payload: Capture the session cookie pre-login, authenticate, and compare values.
variants.expect: Post-login value differs; the old id is rejected on the next request.
variants.why: The direct fixation test on your own accounts.

variants.name: Plant your own id
variants.payload: Set the session cookie to a known pre-auth value you obtained, log in, and check whether the server keeps it.
variants.expect: Server replaces it — an accepted planted id is textbook session fixation.
variants.why: This is the attacker replay of the same rule, done safely with your own test account.

variants.name: Old id replay
variants.payload: Re-issue a request with the pre-login id after authenticating.
variants.expect: Pre-login id has no authenticated authority anywhere.
variants.why: Killing the old id closes the fixation window.

checks.title: Sessions rotate on privilege change
checks.why: Step-up (MFA verify, login-as, admin elevation, role grant) must reissue authority — otherwise a pre-elevation cookie from an XSS or log can be replayed as elevated.
checks.validate: Every privilege or assurance change issues a new session token and invalidates the previous one.

variants.name: Step-up compare
variants.payload: Complete an MFA step-up or sensitive re-auth; compare session cookie before/after.
variants.expect: New value; old token rejected immediately.
variants.why: Elevation is exactly when old authority must die.

variants.name: Old-elevation replay
variants.payload: Capture the pre-elevation token, elevate, then replay the old token on an elevated endpoint.
variants.expect: Old token cannot reach elevated functions.
variants.why: The finding that matters: replay after elevation.

variants.name: Role grant timing
variants.payload: With owner approval, grant your test account a new role mid-session, then inspect the token and its reach.
variants.expect: Either the token refreshes or server-side roles are re-evaluated per request; stale elevated reach is a finding.
variants.why: Privilege changes mid-life are common — cache windows become privilege windows.

checks.title: No session puzzling across token names
checks.why: When several cookie or parameter names can carry authority (legacy + current, access + SSO), the server may mix them: identity from one, permissions from another.
checks.validate: Exactly one authority source per request; superseded names are ignored, not merged.

variants.name: Duplicate names
variants.payload: Send both the legacy session name and the current one with different accounts (both yours).
variants.expect: Server honors exactly one (documented); no mixed identity in responses.
variants.why: Two live authorities is one too many.

variants.name: Token in multiple transports
variants.payload: Provide the session via cookie AND header/body parameter with conflicting values.
variants.expect: One transport wins consistently; the other is ignored — never merged.
variants.why: Transport duplication invites parser-split confusion.

variants.name: Empty-vs-stale precedence
variants.payload: Send current-name empty with legacy-name valid (and the reverse).
variants.expect: Missing current token means unauthenticated, regardless of legacy values.
variants.why: Empty must not fall through to stale authority.

checks.title: Authority isolated across sibling apps
checks.why: Parent-domain session cookies make every subdomain a session holder: the weakest sibling becomes the auth bypass for the strongest app.
checks.validate: Application session authority is scoped to its host (or an explicitly hardened SSO domain) and is not accepted by siblings.

variants.name: Cross-host replay
variants.payload: Take the app session cookie and send it to a sibling subdomain in scope (different first-party app).
variants.expect: Sibling rejects it — different issuer, different key, different audience.
variants.why: The direct cross-app replay with your own token.

variants.name: Scope attribute evidence
variants.payload: Read Domain on the session cookie and map every host that would receive it.
variants.expect: Only intended hosts; parent-scoped authority documented as accepted risk or fixed.
variants.why: The attribute tells you the exposure before any request.

variants.name: Cookie-shadowing
variants.payload: From a sibling subdomain in scope, set a same-named cookie and revisit the main app.
variants.expect: Main app does not adopt sibling-set values for authority (host-only scoping prevents the shadow).
variants.why: Sibling-writable session names let a weaker host plant sessions.

checks.title: No session adoption on account switch
checks.why: Logout-login as another user (or admin login-as) must not carry over carts, impersonation context, or MFA state from the previous identity.
checks.validate: Switching accounts starts a clean session: no carry-over of identity-bound state, and login-as is time-boxed and marked.

variants.name: A to B carry-over
variants.payload: As test account A, put a marker in identity-bound state (cart item, draft); log out, log in as B, and look for the marker.
variants.expect: Session B has none of account A state.
variants.why: Leaked cross-account state is a cross-user disclosure.

variants.name: Logout completeness
variants.payload: After logout, immediately re-issue an authenticated request with the old cookie.
variants.expect: Rejected; logout kills the server-side session, not just the client copy.
variants.why: The oldest logout rule, still the most commonly broken.

variants.name: Login-as hygiene
variants.payload: If admins can impersonate: use it on your own test account; inspect session marking and exit path.
variants.expect: Impersonation uses a distinct, time-boxed session with audit trail and a clean exit back to admin.
variants.why: Login-as is powerful; its session must say so.

checks.title: Concurrent session limits enforced
checks.why: Unlimited parallel sessions defeat anomaly response and share credentials silently; policy must actually be enforced server-side.
checks.validate: Documented concurrent-session limit (or deliberate unlimited policy) enforced on login, with the older session handling defined.

variants.name: N-browser login
variants.payload: Log in from 3+ separate browser profiles/containers as the same test account.
variants.expect: Behaviour matches policy: either a cap with oldest-session eviction or a documented unlimited decision.
variants.why: Parallel logins on your own account are the whole test.

variants.name: Eviction effect
variants.payload: When the cap evicts, re-use the evicted session.
variants.expect: Evicted session is rejected — eviction is server-side, not cosmetic.
variants.why: Eviction that leaves the old cookie working is UI fiction.

variants.name: Notification check
variants.payload: Observe whether new logins notify the user (email/in-app) where policy promises it.
variants.expect: Notification fires as documented for the report.
variants.why: Detection complements prevention.

checks.title: Users can review and revoke sessions
checks.why: A session list with one-click revoke is the user-side incident response for stolen cookies.
checks.validate: A settings page lists active sessions (device, location, time) and revoking one takes effect immediately.

variants.name: Inventory accuracy
variants.payload: Log in from two distinct browsers; open the sessions page.
variants.expect: Both sessions listed with usable metadata; no phantom or missing entries.
variants.why: You cannot revoke what you cannot see.

variants.name: Revoke other session
variants.payload: From browser A, revoke the browser-B session; then re-issue a request in B.
variants.expect: Next request in B is unauthenticated — immediately, not on next login.
variants.why: The revocation race matters: prove immediacy.

variants.name: Metadata honesty
variants.payload: Check listed details against what you know (user agent, IP, time).
variants.expect: Accurate enough for a user to spot an intruder; fabricated or empty metadata is reportable.
variants.why: The feature is only useful if the data is real.

checks.title: Server-enforced inactivity timeout
checks.why: Idle sessions on shared or compromised machines are free access; the server must expire them, not a client-side timer.
checks.validate: After the documented idle window, the next request requires re-auth regardless of client behaviour.

variants.name: Idle then request
variants.payload: With the documented idle window known, stop all traffic, wait it out plus margin, then re-request an authenticated endpoint with the old cookie.
variants.expect: 401/redirect to login; server-side expiry proven.
variants.why: Patient version: respect the window rather than hammering.

variants.name: Client-timer bypass
variants.payload: Keep the tab closed but re-issue the request via Repeater at the same moment a browser heartbeat would have fired.
variants.expect: No JS-heartbeat exemption: server time rules.
variants.why: Heartbeats that never touch server-side expiry defeat the policy.

variants.name: Partial-activity note
variants.payload: Record which requests do and do not reset the idle clock (polling, assets, websocket frames).
variants.expect: Idle clock driven by meaningful authenticated activity per policy; background noise renewing sessions forever is a finding.
variants.why: Define activity or the timeout is decorative.

checks.title: Absolute maximum session lifetime
checks.why: Even active sessions must die at an absolute cap, or one stolen cookie lives as long as the account is never idle.
checks.validate: A hard maximum age is enforced server-side regardless of activity.

variants.name: Stay-alive marathon
variants.payload: Keep the session lightly active (one harmless request every few minutes) past the documented maximum age.
variants.expect: Session terminates at the cap and requires re-auth.
variants.why: Activity must not extend life beyond the ceiling.

variants.name: Cap discovery
variants.payload: Where policy is unknown, run the stay-alive pattern in bounded steps (30m, 1h, 8h — engagement time permitting) or read documentation.
variants.expect: Documented observed bound for the report; never-expiring is the finding.
variants.why: Measure, do not assume.

variants.name: Re-auth token swap
variants.payload: After the cap forces re-auth, confirm a fresh session id is issued.
variants.expect: New session value — the cap is a lifecycle boundary, not a client refresh.
variants.why: Re-auth that recycles the old id re-opens fixation surface.

checks.title: Expiry enforced server-side
checks.why: Client-controlled timestamps (cookie Max-Age, embedded exp claims, hidden fields) must never be the authority for session validity.
checks.validate: Validity is decided by server-side state (or a cryptographically bound exp): tampering with client timestamps changes nothing.

variants.name: Cookie clock stretch
variants.payload: Edit the session cookie Expires/Max-Age in DevTools to +30 days; re-issue an authenticated request.
variants.expect: Server still enforces its own expiry; the attribute is transport, not authority.
variants.why: Cookie attributes are client input.

variants.name: Embedded exp tamper
variants.payload: If the token embeds exp/issued-at (JWT-style), modify them (expect signature failure) or replay an expired reference token.
variants.expect: Expired is expired: 401 either way.
variants.why: Signature-protected exp is fine; trust-by-readout is not.

variants.name: Logout-timer race
variants.payload: Log out, then immediately replay the cookie before any client cleanup.
variants.expect: Rejected — server-side invalidation is instant.
variants.why: The server, not the browser, decides death.

checks.title: No session authority in script-readable storage
checks.why: localStorage/sessionStorage tokens are one XSS away from theft with no HttpOnly protection.
checks.validate: Session authority lives in HttpOnly cookies or memory; web storage holds nothing that restores authenticated state.

variants.name: Storage sweep
variants.payload: DevTools Application tab: local/session storage on the authed app; decode JWT-shaped values.
variants.expect: No identity-restoring material; document anything found with its reach.
variants.why: The five-minute inventory that maps XSS blast radius.

variants.name: Script-reachability proof
variants.payload: In the console, read the stored keys and replay one into an Authorization header on a harmless endpoint.
variants.expect: Nothing in storage grants authenticated responses.
variants.why: Proves reachability rather than just presence.

variants.name: Logout residue
variants.payload: After logout, re-sweep storage.
variants.expect: All session material removed.
variants.why: Left-behind tokens outlive the session they served.

checks.title: Disabled and deleted accounts replay nothing
checks.why: Account disablement is the incident-response switch; live sessions for disabled users defeat it entirely.
checks.validate: Disabling or deleting an account invalidates all its sessions immediately (within the documented propagation window).

variants.name: Disable-then-replay
variants.payload: With owner approval, disable your test account while holding an active session; immediately re-issue authenticated requests.
variants.expect: 401/403 within the documented window; a working session after disablement is critical.
variants.why: The exact incident-response scenario, on an account you own.

variants.name: Delete-then-replay
variants.payload: Same pattern with account deletion (or anonymization) if policy allows test accounts to be removed.
variants.expect: All sessions dead; deleted identities cannot authenticate anywhere.
variants.why: Deletion must be stronger than disablement, never weaker.

variants.name: Scheduled-window note
variants.payload: If revocation propagates (multi-node), measure the window by hitting a second node/region quickly.
variants.expect: Propagation matches the documented bound; record it as the honest revocation SLA.
variants.why: Distributed systems get a window — it must be known.

checks.title: Password and factor changes end other sessions
checks.why: Changing a password is what a user does when they suspect compromise; surviving stolen sessions make the ritual meaningless.
checks.validate: Password change (and factor add/remove) revokes other sessions, or offers explicit revocation that works.

variants.name: Change-then-other-session
variants.payload: Hold sessions in two browsers; change the password in A; re-issue in B.
variants.expect: B is logged out (or explicitly offered revocation that works immediately).
variants.why: The user story: I changed my password — am I safe now?

variants.name: Factor-change parity
variants.payload: Add or remove an MFA factor; check other sessions.
variants.expect: Same revocation semantics as password change per policy.
variants.why: Factor changes are compromise responses too.

variants.name: Post-change token freshness
variants.payload: Inspect the session cookie in the browser that made the change.
variants.expect: Fresh session issued (rotation on credential change).
variants.why: The surviving session should at least be new.

checks.title: Local and federated logout coordinated
checks.why: With federation, logging out of the SP while the IdP session lives means one click back in — and SLO that misses either side leaves sessions alive.
checks.validate: Logout offers/propagates SLO where supported; local fallback sessions are cleaned; residual IdP behaviour matches policy.

variants.name: SP logout then IdP state
variants.payload: Log out of the SP; visit the IdP profile page in the same browser.
variants.expect: IdP session per policy (SLO propagated, or documented local-only logout with its risk).
variants.why: Show what a shared-machine attacker retains.

variants.name: SLO round trip
variants.payload: Trigger SLO from the IdP side; sweep SP cookies and re-issue requests.
variants.expect: All SP sessions in scope terminate; post-logout redirect is validated and closed.
variants.why: Both halves of the logout must land.

variants.name: Re-login friction
variants.payload: After full logout, hit the SP login again.
variants.expect: Fresh authentication required — no silent SSO re-entry contradicting the logout.
variants.why: One-click return after logout surprises users and auditors.

checks.title: Sessions only on explicit user action
checks.why: Silent session creation (IdP-initiated SSO landing, token-in-URL auto-login) enables login phishing: a link the victim clicks logs them into an attacker-shaped context.
checks.validate: Application sessions require an explicit interaction at the SP; unsolicited SSO is a documented decision, not a default.

variants.name: Link-driven auto-login
variants.payload: Craft a link (your own test IdP/app flow) that carries a valid assertion/token to the SP without a click at the SP.
variants.expect: SP requires initiation or shows explicit consent before a session exists.
variants.why: The phishing primitive: authentication without intent.

variants.name: IdP-initiated policy
variants.payload: If IdP-initiated SSO is supported, verify Audience+Issuer strictness and document why it is allowed.
variants.expect: Strict audience binding; the allowance is a written decision.
variants.why: Supported features need reasons.

variants.name: Token-in-URL auto-login
variants.payload: Check proxy history for any login flow that accepts tokens in query/fragment and creates sessions on GET.
variants.expect: No URL-borne session creation; sessions start at POST/redirect exchanges.
variants.why: GET-logins leak via Referer and history.

checks.title: Revocation propagates within the window
checks.why: Logout or revoke must beat the attacker everywhere: caches and second nodes honoring dead sessions extend the compromise window.
checks.validate: After revocation, all endpoints and nodes reject the token within the documented window.

variants.name: Two-endpoint race
variants.payload: Revoke a session; immediately alternate requests between two different endpoints (or regions) with the dead token.
variants.expect: Both reject within the documented propagation bound; measure and record it.
variants.why: The cache that forgot the logout is where sessions resurrect.

variants.name: Cache-layer probe
variants.payload: If a CDN caches authenticated responses, revoke and re-request.
variants.expect: No cached authenticated content served post-revocation (Cache-Control private/no-store).
variants.why: Revocation of identity is also a caching question.

variants.name: Propagation budget note
variants.payload: Compare the measured window against the documented SLA.
variants.expect: Measured within documented; otherwise a finding with the numbers.
variants.why: SLAs are testable statements.

checks.title: Rotated cookie families detect replay
checks.why: Rotating persistent/remember-me cookies on every use, with reuse-revocation, is the refresh-token lesson applied to cookies.
checks.validate: Persistent session cookies rotate per use; replaying a rotated cookie revokes the family.

variants.name: Rotated-cookie replay
variants.payload: With remember-me enabled, capture cookie P1; make another request (P1 to P2); then replay P1 from a second client.
variants.expect: P1 rejected and the family (P2) revoked — reuse is treated as theft.
variants.why: Mirror of the JWT refresh-family test, cookie edition.

variants.name: Parallel use race
variants.payload: Fire two requests with P1 simultaneously (Repeater parallel groups, 2-3 max).
variants.expect: At most one rotation wins linearly; no parallel families issued.
variants.why: Rotation must be atomic under concurrency.

variants.name: Family-scope check
variants.payload: Confirm the revocation hits sibling sessions of the same family, not the whole account.
variants.expect: Scope matches policy (family-wide vs account-wide) and is documented.
variants.why: Blast radius of reuse-revocation should be a decision.

sess-cookie.purpose: The Secure flag on the session cookie is the transport protection.
sess-cookie.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password=ChangeMe1!

doc-cookie.purpose: A session cookie readable from document.cookie is exposed to any XSS.
doc-cookie.payload: In the logged-in origin console: document.cookie
